questions.q: Which is a non-monetary consideration in choosing a job?
questions.why: Satisfaction, conditions and hours are not paid in money.

questions.q: A rise in the wage for a job causes:
options: A movement along the supply curve of labour
A shift of the supply curve to the right
A shift of the supply curve to the left
A shift of the demand curve
questions.why: A change in the job's own wage is a movement along its curve.

questions.q: Match each change to its effect on the supply of labour to nursing.
questions.why: Anything other than the job's own wage shifts the curve.

questions.q: The supply curve of labour to an occupation slopes upwards.
questions.why: Higher pay attracts more workers to the job.

questions.q: Why might a dangerous job pay more than a safe one with the same skills?
options: The supply of labour to it is lower
Demand for it is always lower
questions.why: Fewer are willing to do it at any given wage, so the wage is pushed up.

questions.q: Explain how better working conditions could affect the wage in an occupation.

ideas.label: More people are willing to do the job, so supply shifts right
This puts downward pressure on the wage

questions.model: Better conditions make the job more attractive, so more people are willing to do it and supply shifts right. With no change in demand, this pushes the wage down.
questions.why: Conditions are part of the reward, so they can replace some pay.

tests.answer: More people want to do the job so supply shifts right, and the wage falls.
